# **Introduction.**

In our project, we are taking the US counties TIGER dataset and allowing users to query for information in it using natural language. From this natural language, we utilized few shot learning to train an LLM to output an SQL statement that produces the answer to the user’s query. This SQL statement is then sent to a POSTGIS database where we get the result and then we display the results to the user. Depending on the query, the frontend either displays a map displaying the result, or provides a table displaying the results of the query.

# **Methodology.**

First we shall start with the database and our initial dataset. This dataset is the US counties 2018 TIGER dataset. This dataset includes all counties in mainland United States as well as counties in Hawaii, the boroughs of Alaska, and the county equivalents in US territories. To put all this into a database, we first gathered all the information we could regarding the columns of the database, then we set the columns and created a POSTGIS database on the dataset. For the most part, we did not employ any special instructions that go beyond the normal action set of making a POSTGIS database other than renaming all the columns to be the lowercase version of their title. This step was taken to allow for SQL statements to be made in an easier fashion as well as make each future SQL statement more readable.

Next we will move onto the LLM and its training. The LLM we decided to train is the Phi-3-Mini-4k-Instruct model which is publically available. This model has 3.8 billion parameters with a maximum context length of 4 thousand tokens, making this a larger model than others. In order to run this model within the time limit of 9 seconds, we had to quantize the model down to 8 bits and allow for flash attention to be utilized. To train this model, we decided to follow a similar approach to the paper “GPT-Based Text-to-SQL for Spatial Databases”. We first create a large prompt which includes telling the model the following in order: that the model is an expert in making POSTGIS SQL statements, a description of some ST functions, some example input and outputs, and the database schema. We also added at the end the description of the columns to help the model understand the dataset. 

The following prompt is what is sent to our model if the user query was “show me all madison counties”:

You are an expert in the PostGIS spatial database and highly skilled in writing SQL queries for geographic analysis.  
PostGIS extends PostgreSQL with spatial data types and functions.  
Below is a quick reference of commonly used spatial functions and their meanings:  
\- ST\_Within(geomA, geomB): Returns TRUE if geometry A is completely within geometry B.  
\- ST\_Intersects(geomA, geomB): Returns TRUE if geometry A and B share any portion of space.  
\- ST\_Distance(geomA, geomB): Returns the minimum distance between geometries A and B, in the same units as the spatial reference system.  
\- ST\_Length(geometry): Returns the length of a LineString in its spatial reference units.  
\- ST\_Area(geometry): Returns the area of a Polygon.  
\- ST\_Contains(geomA, geomB): Returns TRUE if geometry A contains geometry B.  
\- ST\_Union(geomA, geomB): Returns a geometry that represents the union of geomA and geomB.  
\- ST\_Centroid(geometry): Returns the geometric center of a geometry.  
\- ST\_Buffer(geometry, distance): Returns a geometry covering all points within a given distance from the input geometry.  
\- ST\_AsText(geometry): Returns the Well-Known Text (WKT) representation of the geometry.

Below are example pairs of natural-language questions (NLQs) and their corresponding SQL queries:  
\[Example-1\]  
NLQ: visualize me madison county in all states  
SQL: SELECT \* FROM counties WHERE name \= 'Madison';  
\[Example-2\]  
NLQ: tell me how many counties are called madison county  
SQL: SELECT COUNT(\*) AS frequency FROM counties WHERE name \= 'Madison';  
\[Example-3\]  
NLQ: show me madison county idaho  
SQL: SELECT \* FROM counties WHERE name \= 'Madison' AND state \= 'Idaho';

Below is the database schema:  
CREATE TABLE counties (  
    "geometry" geometry(GEOMETRY,4326),  
    "statefp" BIGINT,  
    "countyfp" BIGINT,  
    "countyns" BIGINT,  
    "geoid" BIGINT,  
    "name" TEXT,  
    "namelsad" TEXT,  
    "lsad" BIGINT,  
    "classfp" TEXT,  
    "mtfcc" TEXT,  
    "csafp" TEXT,  
    "cbsafp" TEXT,  
    "metdivfp" TEXT,  
    "funcstat" TEXT,  
    "aland" BIGINT,  
    "awater" BIGINT,  
    "intptlat" DOUBLE PRECISION,  
    "intptlon" DOUBLE PRECISION,  
    "state" TEXT,  
    "stateaabrv" TEXT  
);

Decription of table columns:

geometry \- polygon for each county  
statefp \- state FIPS code  
countyfp \- county FIPS code  
countyns \- county GNIS/ANSI code  
geoid \- combined state+county FIPS  
name \- county name  
namelsad \- full county name including legal/statistical descriptor  
lsad \- legal/statistical area descriptor code  
classfp \- county class code  
mtfcc \- MAF/TIGER feature class code  
csafp \- central statistical area FIPS code  
cbsafp \- core-based statistical area FIPS code  
metdivfp \- metropolitan division FIPS code  
funcstat \- functional status of county (active/inactive)  
aland \- land area in square meters  
awater \- water area in square meters  
intptlat \- internal point latitude (centroid)  
intptlon \- internal point longitude (centroid)  
state \- full state name  
stateaabrv \- state two-letter abbreviation

Answer the following with no explanation:  
NLQ: show me all madison counties

	To provide the model quality examples that resemble the user’s query, we first needed to create training data. This data is in the form of a query and the resulting SQL answer. To make this data, we used GPT-5 to create a large batch and then handmade several data points as well. The data generated by GPT-5 was then put through a large verification process in order to ensure the SQL was perfect (perfect in the sense that this SQL is exactly what the user wants and will not produce an error when fed into the database). After that, we followed the original paper and performed masked schema embedding on all the questions in the dataset. This is so we can retain the relative meaning of the questions (in tests, we observed that these embeddings are extremely close to normal BERT embeddings).

	To train the model, we simply allow first the user to make a query, then we perform masked schema embedding and masked state embedding on the query and perform cosine similarity to our training dataset. To perform masked schema embedding, we simply mask words in the query that are the same as our database schema, this process is also similar to masked state embedding where we do the same thing but for the name of states (this was done in tests where we see the returned examples have higher scores simply because the state matched).  From this we extract the three data points that are the closest match and put them in as our inputs into the prompt that we send to the LLM. These examples are what the model will base the ending SQL statement on. The reason we chose three is firstly to not overwhelm the model with too much noise and secondly is to keep inference time low. By doing this prompt engineering, we were able to confirm our model was able to make a normal SQL query a majority of the time. 	To build the prompt, we send the query into a prompt builder server which is run on google colab using a basic requests module and ngrok (a service that provides tokens to host servers on google colab). 

Now, to produce the LLM result and the final prompt sent to the LLM, we first take the user query and send it to our prompt builder server, this returns the final prompt and then we send that to the LLM server. Before the prompt is executed, we apply a small sanitization step designed to prevent simple avoidable runtime errors. The sanitizer handles four situations:

* SELECT \* cases remain unchanged  
* Queries containing aggregate functions, where we insert or repair GROUP BY clauses, making sure that non-aggregate columns are valid  
* Spatial analytic queries involving joins and ST functions, where we ensure the geometry column is included and properly grouped.  
* Standard non-aggregate queries, where we simply add the geometry column if it is missing and it does not have a qualified asterisk.

These changes avoid unnecessary exceptions being sent back to the model when minor adjustments can be made.

	The LLM is hosted on our LLM server where we host the server on google colab using the basic request module and ngrok as well. This server is set to a specific directory in google drive as it takes advantage of storing the wheels of our required packages, making it faster to install. This model also requires the hardware selected to be either the A100 GPU or the L4 GPU. 

	For our frontend, we utilized streamlit to create a basic front end where we allow the user a small interface to place a query and button for them to submit the query. Once the user submits a query, we use a basic requests module to contact our servers to both build the prompt and to send that prompt to our model. The model will then respond and the resulting SQL will be sanitized and sent back to our local system. Where then we run the SQL using psycopg2 to connect to our database and run the SQL. Then we check if the result has the column “geometry” in it. If it does then we run the SQL in geopandas to have a geopandas result. This we found was easier to implement with folium which we use then to generate our map. If the result does not contain “geometry” then we simply display the table result. After we display the result in either form, we store the result, query, prompt, and time that it takes for each task in the system. We then store this information in the query log. If there is a case where there are no results or the model produces SQL that is incorrect, we simply display no results. 

# **Illustration of complete product pipeline.**

![][image2]  
	Here is a complete illustration of our product pipeline. First we get a user query, then we send this user query to our prompt builder server using a basic requests module. This returns the prompt that is first sent to the local machine then we send this prompt to the LLM server. The LLM produces the SQL and within the same server, we send the SQL to the SQL sanitizer function we made. Then we return the clean SQL to the local machine where it runs the SQL in the database. If the result of that has geometry, we make another query in geopandas and render the result in a folium map, if not then we simply display the table result.

# **Deployment Instructions.**

	To deploy our project, first launch the LLM\_SERVER.ipynb in google colab and allow it to run all cells. Ensure that this server is run with an L4 GPU. Then launch the PROMPT\_BUILDER.ipynb in google colab as well (this can be launched on a CPU) and upload the training data (ensure the file is called “Training\_Data.csv”) prior to running the prompt builder server. When both servers are up and running, then launch the frontend using streamlit app.py. Then when the frontend is visible, open the database settings on the left and click “Connect to database”. Once the database is connected, the system is ready to be used.  
	Please do note, our servers are run using ngrok which provides a personalized authentication token. These tokens may not function if the token is deleted on ngrok’s website. As such we highly recommend making your own ngrok account and authentication token and replacing it in our code.
